newsitem.title: UK: Oil sheds gains as market succumbs to bearish tone.
newsitem.headline: Oil sheds gains as market succumbs to bearish tone.

text.p: Oil markets succumbed to bearish underlying fundamentals on Wednesday, shedding early gains made in the wake of news of a higher than expected draw on U.S. gasoline stocks last week.
The first clear signs of concern from OPEC ministers about this year's slump in prices also helped give the market an early shot in the arm, traders said.
World benchmark Brent blend crude oil futures for prompt delivery, which have shed over $7 a barrel since early January, fell 20 cents to close at $17.73 a barrel, way off the day's high of $18.34.
Traders said that a break through the key support level of $18.00 triggered technical selling orders, hastening the slide.
"We went through support at $18.03 then (psychologically important) $18.00 and then the stops got triggered," a broker on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) said.
Most of the early gains were attributed to bullish weekly U.S. oil inventory data which showed a widening year-on-year deficit in gasoline stocks with the peak summer driving season fast approaching.
Industry and government data showed U.S. gasoline stocks fell by about 1.2 million barrels last week, leaving them nearly six million barrels adrift from year-ago levels.
"Overall the figures are slightly positive, led by the strength of gasoline demand," said brokers GNI in a daily report.

Shaken oil markets, which have plummeted this year on a combination of renewed Iraqi exports, OPEC quota-busting, robust non-OPEC supply growth and lacklustre winter demand for heating fuel, also drew modest support from evidence the slide was beginning to stir the cartel into action.

The president of the 11-strong Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), Libyan oil minister Abdalla el-Badri, has been consulting this week with his ministerial counterparts about the oil price weakness.
"There has been some contact this week. He was planning to call all the ministers," said an OPEC delegate.
OPEC ministers have watched the value of their crude oil exports dive by about 30 percent since the turn of the year, putting renewed pressure on national budgets.
OPEC giant Saudi Arabia, having enjoyed a $12 billion budget windfall from last year's unexpectedly high prices, raised its 1997 budget projection for a barrel of Saudi crude by $2 to $16-$16.50.
Its main export stream, Arab Light, on Wednesday was valued at just $15 for European buyers.
Despite the potential for a budget squeeze, OPEC delegates and officials said the group remains extremely unlikely to take any action ahead of their next scheduled conference in Vienna on June 25.
And some analysts say it will not be long before healthy stocks and ample supply of crude oil in the Atlantic Basin start to depress prices again.
Traders pointed out that total U.S. crude imports last week stood at 8.3 million bpd, the highest level since October 1996.

For the first time in five years, second quarter non-OPEC supply should exceed first quarter levels, thanks to new start-ups, repairs and upgrades to North Sea fields and accelerating Latin American production, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said earlier this week.
"Fundamentals still don't look that great but they aren't the only thing that determines prices," said Scott Carter, senior trader at Tosco Petroleum in London.
